defs_parts: Eight labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow.
In the book text: the course text uses and explains the term.
In the glossary: the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it.
Editor or docs: the term comes from the editor itself or its official documentation.
Video only: the term comes from a video lecture, and is not in the course text or on the term list.
Computed: the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs.
Simulation: a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game.
Illustrative data: numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured.
Conceptual: a drawing of the idea, with no data behind it.
recap_lines: Resolution is pixels in the file, the viewport is pixels the game draws into.
Pixel art needs Nearest on the node and whole-number scaling.
A sprite sheet is the image, and SpriteFrames is the resource that plays it.
Cut the background to alpha zero, and never prompt for a transparent one.
The collider is sized from the body and kept apart from the art.
A loop point repeats, a one-shot stops, and headroom keeps a mix from clipping.
bookends.command: Give me short cases from making a two D game, one at a time, about its art and sound. Each case should turn on one of these terms, resolution, viewport, nearest vs linear, sprite sheet, SpriteFrames, mipmaps, loop point, one-shot, headroom or clipping. I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Wait for my reply before you give the answer.
checks: Check: each case is a game-making situation, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike was wrong.
